title: Bank and insurance unions: the NOBW, the NOBO and the public sector
author: Editorial Desk
summary: How public sector banking came about, the mergers of 2017-2020, the issues bank unions raise, and why BMS argues that public sector banks have a social role.
body:
Banking is one of the few sectors in which almost every citizen meets the workforce face to face. The clerk at the counter, the officer who sanctions a loan and the manager who visits a village are all employees of institutions whose structure has been argued over for more than fifty years. BMS has two federations in the sector, the **National Organisation of Bank Workers (NOBW)** and the **National Organisation of Bank Officers (NOBO)**, and a third body, listed on its website as Insurance Sector Unions. This post explains the background, the issues that bank unions raise and BMS's reasoning on the role of public sector banks.

## How public sector banking came about

Public ownership of banks is a decision that was taken on a particular day. According to Wikipedia's account, the Government nationalised fourteen major commercial banks, each with reserves above Rs 50 crore, with effect from midnight on **19 July 1969**. Together they held about 85 per cent of the country's bank deposits. Parliament passed the enabling law within two weeks, and it received the President's assent on 9 August 1969. Six more banks were nationalised in 1980, after which the Government controlled around 91 per cent of banking business. By 1991, public sector banks accounted for about ninety per cent of the sector.

The reasons given were about reach and direction. Banks that had mainly served large industrial houses and cities were expected to lend to farmers, small industries and weaker sections, and to open branches in places where there was no bank. Whatever one thinks of the results, this is the origin of the argument BMS makes today, that public sector banks have a social role as well as a commercial one.

## Consolidation, not just privatisation

The recent history has been about consolidation. Wikipedia records that on 1 April 2017 five associate banks of the State Bank of India and Bharatiya Mahila Bank were merged into SBI. Vijaya Bank and Dena Bank were merged into Bank of Baroda, effective April 2019. Then on 1 April 2020 four further mergers took effect: Oriental Bank of Commerce and United Bank of India into Punjab National Bank, Syndicate Bank into Canara Bank, Andhra Bank and Corporation Bank into Union Bank of India, and Allahabad Bank into Indian Bank. Wikipedia's list of public sector banks now shows twelve.

For employees, each merger raises practical questions: seniority lists, postings, branch closures, service conditions that were different in the older institutions, and the workload on branches that suddenly serve a larger customer base. Unions generally ask that such transitions are made with consultation and that no employee loses service benefits.

## The issues unions bring to the table

Bank employees' pay and conditions are not set by individual banks. They are negotiated between the Indian Banks' Association, which represents managements, and the unions, in what is known as a bipartite settlement. That is why bank unions work in forums and why their demands tend to be shared across unions of different affiliations. The recurring issues are:

- **Wage revision** through bipartite settlements, with attention to the pension and family pension arrangements of retirees.
- **The five-day week.** Alternate Saturdays off became a recurring negotiation item, because bank employees wanted a working week comparable to other offices. It is a good example of an issue where the union side, management and the Government all have to agree before anything changes.
- **Recruitment.** Vacancies at the clerical and subordinate levels increase the load on those who remain.
- **Outsourcing** of tasks that were done by regular staff, including in core banking functions.
- **Privatisation and merger** of public sector banks.
- **Safety and conduct at work,** including relations with customers and with supervisors, which are raised by the officers' federation as well as the workers'.

We have not set out the figures of the latest settlement here, because they are best read in the settlement text and the bank associations' own releases.

## BMS's position

BMS argues that public sector banks have a social role. They have been the main channel for schemes of financial inclusion. The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, announced on 15 August 2014 and launched on 28 August 2014, shows this: Wikipedia records over 50 crore accounts by August 2023, and in a table dated August 2022 public sector banks held about 79 per cent of the beneficiaries (36.45 out of 46.30 crore) and about 77 per cent of the deposits. Private banks may do part of the work, but it was the public sector that opened the large majority of those accounts, many in rural branches.

On that basis BMS has opposed the privatisation of public sector banks and insurance companies, and has asked that, in any restructuring, the interests of the employees are protected. It does not argue that nothing in banking should change. It argues that the strategic choice, of who owns banks that act as the main channel between savings and credit in rural India, should not be made merely on the criterion of immediate profit. It also takes the view that private ownership has its own problems; critics, as noted in Wikipedia's account of nationalisation, have pointed to aggressive recovery practices in loans for homes, vehicles and personal needs.

## In the customer's interest

BMS also says that more staff and better working conditions mean better service. A branch that is short of clerks makes its customers wait, and the shortfall is often visible to anyone who has stood in a queue. Officers who carry heavy targets, and have to sell products as well as lend, have less time for the customer. Better staffing is therefore not only a union demand but a quality-of-service measure.

This is the sense in which the issue of bank employees is a public issue and not only a union issue. When a pensioner in a small town cannot get a passbook updated, or a small trader waits weeks for a loan decision, the explanation often lies in staffing and workload.

## What remains to be done

- A fair and timely **wage settlement**, with improvements in retirement benefits.
- Progress on the **five-day week**, which has been negotiated for years.
- **Recruitment** to fill vacancies, so that branches are adequately staffed.
- **Consultation** before any further merger or change of ownership.
- Work on the **social role** of the banks: rural branches, loans to small borrowers and help for first-time account holders.

The test of any reform in banking, in the end, is whether the person at the counter and the person on the other side of it are both better off.
